q: What are the oldest known puzzles?
What is the Sam Loyd puzzle?
Who created the first jigsaw puzzle?
a: Ancient puzzles date back thousands of years: the Archimedes Stomachion (a dissection puzzle dating to around 250 BCE) challenged solvers to arrange 14 irregular polygonal pieces into a square, while tangrams originated in China during the Song Dynasty (960-1279 CE) and became wildly popular in Europe and America during the 19th century as a parlor game. The 1890s puzzle craze was sparked by Sam Loyd's notorious 14-15 puzzle (a sliding tile puzzle that appeared to require an impossible parity swap, leading to an international obsession that was mathematically proven unsolvable), and John Spilsbury created the first jigsaw puzzle in 1767 by mounting a map on mahogany and cutting along country borders, originally intended as a geography teaching tool.

q: What was the first crossword puzzle?
When was the Rubik's Cube invented?
How did Erno Rubik invent the cube?
a: Arthur Wynne invented the crossword puzzle in 1913 for the New York World's Sunday supplement, drawing a diamond-shaped grid with no internal black squares and numbering the clues by row rather than the modern coordinate system, and it became an instant success that spawned countless imitations worldwide. Ernő Rubik, a Hungarian architecture professor, invented the Rubik's Cube in 1974 as a three-dimensional teaching tool for demonstrating spatial relationships to his students, not initially realizing he had created the world's best-selling puzzle toy—it took him over a month to solve his own creation the first time, and over 350 million cubes have been sold worldwide since its mass production in 1980.

q: What was the puzzle boom of the 20th century?
Who were the most important puzzle authors?
What were the first internet puzzles?
puzzle books Martin Gardner Smullyan Dudeney
puzzle phenomenon Portal Witness Baba Is You
a: The 20th century puzzle boom was driven by influential authors and puzzle creators: Martin Gardner's 'Mathematical Games' column in Scientific American (1956-1981) introduced millions to mathematical puzzles, flexagons, and recreational mathematics, Raymond Smullyan created brilliant logic puzzles and retrograde analysis chess problems in books like 'What Is the Name of This Book?,' and Henry Dudeney (the 19th-20th century English puzzle creator) authored 'The Canterbury Puzzles' and 'Amusements in Mathematics,' establishing many puzzle forms still used today. The internet created new puzzle forms including the graphical adventure game 'Myst' (1993), which was the best-selling PC game of its era and defined exploration-based puzzle design, alternate reality games (ARGs) like 'The Beast' (2001) that blend online and real-world puzzles, and modern puzzle games like 'The Witness' (massive open-world environmental puzzles), 'Portal' (physics-based spatial challenges), and 'Baba Is You' (programming-language-style logic puzzles where you can change the rules) that represent the cutting edge of puzzle game design.

q: What was the puzzle craze of the 1890s?
What is the history of puzzle publications?
What were the first puzzle books?
a: The 1890s puzzle craze began with Sam Loyd's 14-15 puzzle, which swept across America and Europe with such intensity that employers posted signs banning it during work hours, as people became obsessed with the (ultimately impossible) challenge of swapping two tiles to create a numerical sequence. Dissected puzzles evolved from educational tools into entertainment products as chromolithography made colorful images affordable to print on wood, and the magic lantern and later photography expanded puzzle themes from maps to fine art reproductions, scenic views, and political cartoons. Puzzle magazines emerged in the early 20th century, with publications like 'The Puzzle Corner' and 'GAMES Magazine' (founded 1977) providing regular puzzle content, while the Dell puzzle magazine line and Penny Press specialized in logic puzzles and fill-in puzzles, creating a publishing category that continues to serve dedicated puzzle solvers in print and digital formats.
